transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A new recycling initiative launched in Vancouver, Canada, is successfully reducing household waste by encouraging residents to separate food scraps for composting. The city-wide program, which began last January, provides all households with special green bins for organic waste, which is collected weekly along with regular garbage and recycling. Since the program started, the amount of waste going to landfills has decreased by approximately 40 percent, and the city has been able to produce large quantities of nutrient-rich compost for use in local parks and community gardens. City officials say the program has exceeded their expectations, with over 90 percent of residents participating regularly. The compost produced is also being sold to local farms and garden centers, generating revenue that helps offset the cost of the program. Vancouver aims to become a zero-waste city by 2040, and officials say this food scrap recycling program is a major step toward achieving that goal. Several other Canadian cities have already sent representatives to study Vancouver's program as a potential model for their own waste management strategies.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: The International Olympic Committee has announced that breakdancing, known officially as "breaking," will make its debut as an Olympic sport at the 2028 Summer Games in Los Angeles. The decision was made after breakdancing was featured as a demonstration sport at the 2024 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal, where it proved extremely popular with both athletes and spectators. Breakdancing, which originated in New York City in the 1970s as part of hip-hop culture, has grown into a competitive sport with organized competitions held around the world. Olympic breakdancing events will feature both men's and women's competitions, with dancers judged on their technical skill, creativity, and musicality. The IOC has been adding newer, more youth-oriented sports in recent years to attract younger audiences and keep the Olympics relevant for future generations. Other new sports added for Los Angeles 2028 include skateboarding, sport climbing, and surfing, which made successful Olympic debuts in Tokyo. Some traditionalists have criticized the addition of these newer sports, arguing that the Olympics should focus on traditional athletic events, but supporters say the changes help modernize the Games.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Female)
paras: A recent study conducted by the American Psychological Association has found that excessive use of social media platforms is linked to increased rates of anxiety and depression among teenagers. The research, which analyzed data from over 12,000 adolescents across the United States, found that teenagers who spent more than seven hours a day on social media were 60 percent more likely to report symptoms of anxiety and depression compared to those who spent less than an hour daily. Even moderate use—between two and three hours per day—was associated with poorer mental health outcomes. The study also found that the effects were more pronounced in girls than in boys, possibly due to higher rates of social comparison and cyberbullying experienced by female users. Researchers say that social media platforms are designed to be highly engaging through features like infinite scrolling and notification alerts, which can disrupt sleep patterns and reduce time spent on healthier activities like exercise and face-to-face social interactions. The study's authors recommend that parents limit their teenagers' social media use to no more than two hours per day and encourage activities that promote mental well-being. They also call on social media companies to take more responsibility for protecting young users by modifying addictive design features.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Lily): Ryan, you look absolutely exhausted. Are you feeling okay?

Man (Ryan): I'm so tired, Lily. I haven't been sleeping well lately. I stay up late every night scrolling through my phone, and then I can't fall asleep because my mind won't shut off. It's starting to affect my grades too—I can barely stay awake in my morning classes.

Woman: Oh, I've had that problem too. Blue light from phone screens really does mess with your sleep cycle. Have you tried putting your phone away an hour before bed? I started doing that a few months ago, and it made such a difference.
Man: I've tried, but I always end up reaching for it anyway. It's become such a habit. Also, I use my phone as my alarm clock, so it's right next to my bed.

Woman: You could get an actual alarm clock! They're like ten dollars at the campus store. That way you don't need to have your phone in your bedroom at all. Or at least put it across the room so you can't reach it from bed. Also, have you tried doing something calming before bed instead, like reading a book or taking a warm bath?

Man: I never really thought about that. I always just scroll through social media until I can't keep my eyes open. But I notice that after I spend time looking at everyone's posts, I feel anxious rather than relaxed.

Woman: That makes sense. A lot of people feel that way. You know, I started using that blue light filter on my phone after 9 PM, and it does help somewhat, but not nearly as much as just not using the phone at all. Also, you might want to avoid drinking coffee or energy drinks after 3 PM—caffeine stays in your system for hours and can make it harder to fall asleep.
Man: Hmm, I definitely have coffee with dinner most nights. That probably doesn't help. Do you have any other suggestions?

Woman: Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. It helps regulate your body's internal clock. Also, make sure your room is dark and quiet—maybe get some blackout curtains if your window faces the street. Oh, and don't study or do work in bed, because your brain will start associating your bed with stress instead of sleep.

Man: Those are really good tips. I'm going to try implementing them starting tonight. First thing tomorrow, I'm going to buy an alarm clock and move my phone charger out of my bedroom. Thanks for all the advice, Lily.
Woman: No problem! Give it a week or two and see how you feel. Getting enough sleep makes such a huge difference in everything—your mood, your grades, even your appetite. You'll be amazed.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Jack): Amelia, I just got an email about the study abroad program information session next week. Are you planning to go?

Woman (Amelia): I'm not sure, Jack. I've always wanted to study abroad, but I'm worried it will delay my graduation. I'm a double major in Political Science and French, and my schedule is already pretty tight.

Man: But if you study in a French-speaking country, wouldn't that count toward your French major? I thought the study abroad office helps you plan your classes so credits transfer. My cousin studied in Spain last year, and all her classes counted toward her Spanish degree. She said it was the best experience of her college career.

Woman: I know the credits would probably transfer, but I'm also worried about the cost. International tuition and living expenses are so expensive. I don't know if I can afford it, even with financial aid.

Man: Actually, there are tons of scholarships specifically for study abroad. My cousin got a scholarship that covered almost all her expenses. And if you go through our university's exchange program, you pay your regular tuition here, not international tuition. That makes it a lot more affordable. You should talk to the study abroad advisors—they know all about funding options.
Woman: Really? I didn't know that about the exchange program tuition. That's a big relief. Where are you thinking of going?

Man: I'm looking at either Japan or South Korea. I'm an East Asian Studies minor, so either would be great for my language skills. They have information about both programs on the study abroad website. The application deadline isn't until October, so there's still plenty of time to decide.

Woman: That sounds amazing. I'd love to go to Paris or maybe Senegal—both would be perfect for practicing French. But I'm also a little nervous about being away from home for a whole semester. I've never traveled outside of Europe before.

Man: I know what you mean, I'm a little nervous too. But everyone I've talked to says that being in a new country helps you become more independent and confident. And there are usually other students from our university at each program, so you won't be completely alone. We could even go to the information session together if you want—that might make it less intimidating.

Woman: You know what? Let's do it. Let's go to the information session together. It can't hurt to learn more about the options, even if I end up deciding not to go. I don't want to miss out on an opportunity just because I'm scared.
Man: That's the spirit! I'll meet you outside the lecture hall at 4 PM on Wednesday. We can go get coffee afterward and talk about what we learn.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, located between Hawaii and California, is the largest accumulation of ocean plastic in the world. Despite its name, the garbage patch is not a solid island of trash that you can walk on. Instead, it consists of an enormous concentration of microplastics—tiny pieces of plastic less than five millimeters in size—floating throughout the water column, from the surface down to the ocean floor. These microplastics come from larger plastic items that have broken down into smaller and smaller pieces over time due to exposure to sunlight and wave action.

The patch was first documented in 1997 by Captain Charles Moore, who discovered it while sailing back to California after a yacht race. Since then, scientists have found that the garbage patch covers an estimated 1.6 million square kilometers—an area about twice the size of Texas, or three times the size of France. The exact size is difficult to measure because the plastic concentrations vary and move with ocean currents. The patch is held together by the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, a system of circular ocean currents that collects debris from across the Pacific Ocean.

The environmental impact of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is significant. Sea turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals often mistake plastic pieces for food, which can lead to injury, poisoning, and starvation. Plastic debris can also transport invasive species to new regions, disrupting marine ecosystems. Additionally, as plastics break down, they release harmful chemicals into the water that can enter the food chain, eventually affecting humans who eat seafood.

Cleaning up the garbage patch is an enormous challenge because of the vast area involved and the small size of most plastic particles. However, several organizations are developing technologies to remove plastic from the ocean, and many countries are implementing policies to reduce single-use plastic production and improve waste management on land. Most scientists agree that preventing plastic from entering the ocean in the first place is the most effective long-term solution. This includes reducing plastic consumption, improving recycling systems, and holding manufacturers responsible for the entire lifecycle of their plastic products.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: The world's first postage stamp, the Penny Black, was introduced in Great Britain in 1840, revolutionizing how mail was sent and paid for. Before the Penny Black, postage was typically paid by the person receiving the letter rather than the sender, and the cost was calculated based on the distance the letter traveled and the number of sheets of paper. This system was expensive, inefficient, and complicated, with postal rates often so high that ordinary people could not afford to send letters regularly.

The reform of the postal system was largely the work of Sir Rowland Hill, a schoolteacher and social reformer who proposed a uniform, affordable postage rate regardless of distance, paid for by the sender using an adhesive stamp. Hill's ideas were initially met with skepticism from postal officials and politicians, but they gained public support, and the Penny Black was officially issued on May 1, 1840. The stamp featured a profile portrait of Queen Victoria and cost exactly one penny, making it affordable for virtually everyone.

The introduction of the Penny Black was an immediate success. Before the reform, about 76 million letters were sent annually in Britain. Just ten years later, that number had jumped to nearly 350 million, as the new system made correspondence accessible to working-class people for the first time. The idea quickly spread to other countries, with Brazil issuing its own stamps in 1843, followed by the United States in 1847, and soon every nation in the world had adopted adhesive postage stamps.

The Penny Black itself is not as rare as one might think—about 68 million were printed. However, examples in perfect condition are highly prized by stamp collectors, with particularly fine specimens selling for tens of thousands of pounds at auction. The stamp is considered one of the most important innovations in the history of communication, as it laid the foundation for the modern postal service. Before postage stamps, communication across distances was prohibitively expensive for most people, which limited social mobility, business opportunities, and the exchange of ideas. The simple invention of the adhesive postage stamp helped connect people across the country and around the world in ways that had never been possible before.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: For decades, scientists have warned that regular physical exercise is essential for maintaining good health. While most people know that exercise helps with weight management and cardiovascular health, research continues to reveal new and surprising benefits of staying physically active throughout life.

One of the most significant recent findings is that exercise appears to have powerful benefits for brain health and cognitive function. Studies have shown that regular aerobic exercise, such as walking, running, or swimming, increases the size of the hippocampus—a brain region crucial for memory and learning. Exercise also stimulates the production of growth factors that help create new brain cells and form new neural connections. For older adults, regular physical activity has been shown to reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease. Even in younger people, exercise improves attention span, creativity, and problem-solving abilities.

Exercise also has profound effects on mental health. When you exercise, your brain releases endorphins, serotonin, and dopamine—neurotransmitters that help regulate mood and reduce feelings of stress and anxiety. Research has found that regular exercise can be as effective as medication for treating mild to moderate depression in many cases, with fewer side effects. Unlike medication, though, exercise provides benefits beyond just treating symptoms—it improves overall physical health and can prevent numerous chronic diseases.

Many people believe that exercise requires intense workouts at a gym or hours of running every week, but research shows that even moderate levels of activity provide significant benefits. The World Health Organization recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week—this translates to just 30 minutes of brisk walking, five days a week. Activities like gardening, dancing, or taking the stairs instead of the elevator all count toward this total. Starting small is better than not starting at all.

The key is finding activities you enjoy so that exercise doesn't feel like a chore. Whether it's playing a sport, going for hikes, taking dance classes, or simply walking with friends, the best exercise routine is one you'll actually stick with long-term. The evidence is clear: making physical activity a regular part of your life is one of the most important things you can do for your physical health, mental well-being, and long-term quality of life.
